title: USDA-APHIS Tropilaelaps quarantine and reporting protocol
content:
USDA-APHIS TROPILAELAPS QUARANTINE AND REPORTING PROTOCOL

REGULATORY CODE:
Tropilaelaps spp. are classified as a federal quarantine pest by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS). 

WHAT TRIGGERS IT:
Detection of any life stage of Tropilaelaps spp. in honey bee colonies or apiaries triggers immediate regulatory action. This includes both suspected and confirmed cases of infestation.

WHO MUST COMPLY:
All beekeepers, apiary operators, and commercial beekeeping supply companies within the United States must comply with this regulation. This includes individuals or entities that transport bees or bee products across state lines, where the presence of Tropilaelaps spp. is suspected or confirmed.

OPERATIONAL REQUIREMENTS:
Upon suspected detection of Tropilaelaps spp., immediate reporting is mandated. Beekeepers must notify both the APHIS regional office and their state apiarist within 24 hours. Movement of suspect colonies is strictly prohibited until laboratory confirmation is received. Affected colonies must be properly quarantined and managed according to APHIS guidelines to prevent further spread.

CONSEQUENCES OF NON-COMPLIANCE:
Failure to report suspected or confirmed cases of Tropilaelaps spp. can result in significant penalties, including fines and potential legal action. Non-compliant entities may also face loss of operational permits, restrictions on movement of bees, and increased scrutiny from regulatory authorities.

CONTACT FOR QUESTIONS:
For further information or inquiries regarding the Tropilaelaps quarantine protocol, please contact the USDA-APHIS regional office or the designated state apiarist. It is crucial to stay informed and compliant to safeguard both local and national pollinator health.

title: California CDFA apiary movement and registration requirements
content:
CALIFORNIA CDFA APIARY MOVEMENT AND REGISTRATION REQUIREMENTS

REGULATORY CODE  
The California Department of Food and Agriculture (CDFA) regulates apiary movement under state agricultural codes. These regulations are designed to protect honeybee health and manage pest populations.

TRIGGERS  
The requirements are triggered by the operation of commercial apiaries in California. Specifically, any apiary with five or more colonies must register annually with the local county agricultural commissioner. Additionally, any inter-county movement of bees must be reported in advance when transporting five or more colonies.

WHO MUST COMPLY  
All commercial beekeepers operating in California who maintain five or more colonies must comply with these regulations. This includes both resident and non-resident beekeepers wishing to move their apiaries across county lines.

OPERATIONAL REQUIREMENTS  
1. Register your apiary annually with your local county agricultural commissioner.  
2. Provide advance notice for the movement of five or more colonies across county lines.  
3. Ensure that all colonies carry appropriate identification placards as mandated by the CDFA. Tampering with these placards is strictly prohibited and subject to prosecution.

CONSEQUENCES OF NON-COMPLIANCE  
Failure to comply with registration and movement notification requirements can lead to substantial fines, legal action, and potential restrictions on future operations. In severe cases, beekeepers may face the confiscation of their colonies and equipment.

CONTACT INFORMATION  
For questions or further clarification regarding apiary movement and registration, please contact the California Department of Food and Agriculture, Apiary Program at (xxx) xxx-xxxx or visit their website for additional resources. Compliance with these regulations is crucial for sustaining a healthy ecosystem and a thriving commercial beekeeping operation.

title: FDA Veterinary Feed Directive — oxytetracycline for AFB suppression
content:
FDA VETERINARY FEED DIRECTIVE – OXYTETRACTERACYCLINE FOR AFB SUPPRESSION

REGULATORY CODE: The use of oxytetracycline in honey bee colonies is regulated under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA) and specifically falls under the Veterinary Feed Directive (VFD) regulations set forth by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

TRIGGER FOR REGULATION: A Veterinary Feed Directive is triggered when a licensed veterinarian prescribes oxytetracycline to be used in the feed of bee colonies for the control of American Foulbrood (AFB) disease. This regulation ensures that the medication is used responsibly and within the framework of a valid Veterinarian-Client-Patient Relationship (VCPR).

WHO MUST COMPLY: All commercial beekeepers and apiary operators using oxytetracycline in their bee feed must comply with the FDA VFD requirements. This includes obtaining a VFD from a licensed veterinarian and ensuring proper documentation of the treatment process.

OPERATIONAL REQUIREMENTS: Beekeepers must secure a VFD from a licensed veterinarian before administering oxytetracycline. The VFD must detail the dosage, duration, and specific use of the medicated feed. Additionally, accurate records of the VFD, treatment dates, and quantities used must be maintained for a minimum of two years. Beekeepers must also ensure that oxytetracycline feed is used according to labeled instructions to prevent antibiotic resistance.

CONSEQUENCES OF NON-COMPLIANCE: Failure to comply with the VFD regulations can result in significant consequences, including but not limited to fines, product recalls, and potential legal action from the FDA. Non-compliance may also adversely affect the health of bee colonies and lead to the spread of AFB, jeopardizing both the beekeeper's operation and the wider beekeeping community.

CONTACT FOR QUESTIONS: For further information or clarification regarding the FDA Veterinary Feed Directive and its application, please contact the Regulatory Affairs Department at [insert internal contact information].

title: EPA label restrictions — formic acid varroa treatment
content:
EPA LABEL RESTRICTIONS — FORMIC ACID VARROA TREATMENT

REGULATORY CODE: The application of formic acid treatments for Varroa mite control is regulated under the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) as administered by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). 

TRIGGERS: Compliance is triggered when using formic acid products specifically labeled for use in beekeeping. All application instructions provided on the EPA-approved label must be strictly adhered to, including temperature limitations, brood-chamber exposure times, and necessary bee hive ventilation requirements.

WHO MUST COMPLY: All commercial beekeepers and suppliers who use formic acid-based treatments must comply with these regulations. This includes manufacturers, distributors, and individual beekeepers applying these treatments to their hives.

OPERATIONAL REQUIREMENTS: Beekeepers must ensure that formic acid treatments are applied within the specific temperature range indicated on the product label. Treatment duration should not exceed the specified time frame in the brood chamber, and adequate ventilation for the hive must be provided to prevent harmful exposure to bees and to ensure treatment efficacy. It is essential to maintain accurate records of usage in accordance with EPA guidelines.

CONSEQUENCES OF NON-COMPLIANCE: Non-compliance with EPA label restrictions is considered a federal violation, which may result in civil penalties, including fines, loss of licensure, and potential criminal charges depending on the severity and intent of the violation. Additionally, improper use could harm bee populations, jeopardizing the beekeeper's operation and reputation.

CONTACT: For questions regarding compliance or specific application methods, please contact the regulatory compliance team at [insert contact information] or the EPA directly at 1-800-832-7828 for more information regarding FIFRA regulations and label requirements.

title: TTB Certificate of Label Approval analog requirements for mead
content:
TTB-MEAD-COFA 

REGULATORY CODE: 27 CFR Part 4 - Labeling and Advertising of Wine

WHAT TRIGGERS IT: The requirement for a Certificate of Label Approval (COLA) from the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB) is triggered when a honey-based fermented beverage exceeds 7% Alcohol by Volume (ABV). This includes mead and cyser products. 

WHO MUST COMPLY: All producers and bottlers of honey-based fermented beverages that contain more than 7% ABV are subject to this regulation. Additionally, honey suppliers providing honey to these producers may also need to demonstrate compliance regarding the traceability of their honey sourcing.

OPERATIONAL REQUIREMENTS: Producers must submit a COLA application to the TTB prior to marketing any product that meets the aforementioned ABV threshold. The application must include accurate product labeling that adheres to TTB guidelines. For those supplying honey, it is important to maintain documentation that supports the traceability of honey sources, as TTB may request this information to ensure compliance.

CONSEQUENCES OF NON-COMPLIANCE: Failure to obtain a COLA prior to product distribution can result in significant penalties, including fines and product seizure. Additionally, honey suppliers who cannot provide traceability documentation may face regulatory scrutiny, which could hinder business operations or lead to legal consequences.

WHO TO CONTACT FOR QUESTIONS: For inquiries regarding the Certificate of Label Approval process or compliance requirements, please contact the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau at their main office or visit their website for additional resources.
